# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

</document>
response:
The arithmetic checks out. The sector figures, employee-weighted mean (98.7), per-hour figures, and percentage changes are all internally consistent. The problems are in what the numbers can support. The main conclusions, especially "sector-general," go beyond the evidence, and several patterns in the paper's own data cut against them.

## Major issues

**1. The "gain in output per hour" is produced by the arithmetic, not observed.**
Output per scheduled hour is just the output index divided by 0.8. Any organisation whose index stayed above 80 will show a per-hour "gain." So "every sector shows a substantial increase" adds no information beyond the output index itself. The 23.4% headline is the 98.7 index restated. The paper should lead with what was measured: output fell 1.3% overall and 6.9% in retail and hospitality. The per-hour figures should be presented as derived and conditional on hours actually falling by 20%.

**2. Actual hours are unknown, so the per-hour figures are an upper bound at best.**
Limitation 4 concedes this, but it directly undermines the headline number. If staff worked on their day off or lengthened their other days, the real per-hour gain is smaller. This matters most where coverage must be maintained, such as the 17 organisations with staggered days off and probably retail and hospitality. Even a modest shortfall changes the picture: if actual hours fell 15% rather than 20%, the gain is about 16%, not 23%.

**3. The paper's own data contradict "sector-general."**
- In retail and hospitality, **3 of 6 organisations reverted (50%)**. In healthcare administration, 2 of 5 reverted (40%). Every organisation in the other four sectors continued.
- These are also the two sectors with the largest output losses (−6.9% and −3.5%).

Together, the output and continuation data point to a gradient: the model works well in office and knowledge work and fits worse in coverage-bound work. That is close to the "common view" the Discussion dismisses. The sample is also small (6 retail organisations, 300 staff), with no variation shown within sectors and no uncertainty intervals. And six sectors that exclude manufacturing, frontline care, education, and logistics cannot establish generality across sectors. "Provided organisations prepare" is untested too, since every organisation prepared.

**4. The stated bargain wasn't met, and unit labour costs rose.**
Hourly pay rose 25% (full pay for 80% of hours). With output at 98.7, unit labour cost rose about 1.3% overall and about 7.4% in retail and hospitality. That may well be worth it given the gains in retention and sickness, but the paper should say so plainly. As written, "100% of the output" is implied to have held when it didn't.

**5. The primary outcome is vulnerable to reporting bias.**
- The output index was filled in by managers who were responsible for the pilot.
- It was based on "whatever records" each organisation held, so it isn't comparable across organisations.
- The protocol explicitly framed success as delivering 100% output.

An index clustering near 100 is what you'd expect whether or not output was truly maintained. Effects of this size (a few points) are well within the plausible range of that bias. Objective output measures for even a subset of organisations would strengthen the paper greatly.

**6. The revenue figure probably signals a real decline.**
Revenue rose 1.4% in nominal terms, year on year. The pilot ran in 2023–24, when inflation in most advanced economies was well above 1.4%, so real revenue likely fell. "No sign that output was sacrificed" is not supported. There are further problems:
- 9 of 61 organisations didn't report revenue, and missingness may not be random.
- "Revenue" is an odd measure for non-profits.
- Revenue uses a different comparison window from the output index (same months of the previous year versus the six months immediately before), so the two can't be read together cleanly.

**7. HR outcomes may be affected by seasonality and labour-market trends.**
Revenue was compared with the same months of the previous year specifically to remove seasonality. Sick days and resignations, however, appear to be annualised six-month figures compared with a baseline whose timing isn't stated. If the baseline included winter, sick days would fall without any intervention. Quit rates were also declining broadly across 2023 as labour markets cooled. With no control group, the 36% and 56% figures can't be attributed to the schedule alone. The paper should state the baseline windows and, ideally, match calendar months.

**8. The fading energy result undercuts the fatigue explanation.**
Energy rose 0.61 SD at month three and fell to 0.29 SD by month six, losing more than half the gain. That pattern fits novelty or Hawthorne effects at least as well as reduced fatigue, and it bears on the duration limitation. Yet the Discussion calls the wellbeing results "consistent" and names fatigue as the most plausible explanation. The design can't separate fatigue from the process changes managers described: fewer meetings, focus blocks, and dropped reporting. The latter is arguably better supported by the paper's own interview evidence (47 of 58 managers mentioned meetings).

**9. Continuation is weak evidence of productivity.**
Organisations that self-selected into the pilot are predisposed to continue. Withdrawing a popular benefit is also costly for morale and retention whatever happened to productivity. Only 18 of 56 made the change permanent, and the status of the other 38 isn't described. The sector pattern of reversals (point 3) is the informative part of this result, and the Discussion doesn't mention it.

## Smaller points

- Survey response rates aren't reported. People who resigned are missing from the month-six survey, which introduces survivorship bias.
- "64% rate own productivity higher than before" has no baseline or comparison and is purely self-report.
- The baseline period (six months before the pilot) appears to overlap the two-month preparation phase, which may have already changed working practices.
- Results are reported only as employee-weighted means. Organisation-level distributions and unweighted means would show whether a few large organisations drive the results.
- The closing judgment that the limitations are "unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency" is circular. The size and consistency of the per-hour figures come from the 0.8 division (point 1), and the limitations (manager reporting, actual hours) bear directly on that result.
- The Summary repeats the revenue and sector-general claims without the caveats given in the body.

## What the evidence supports

A fairer summary would read something like this:

> Organisations reported output close to baseline (98.7) after a 20% cut in scheduled hours, with larger shortfalls and more reversals in customer-facing sectors. Per-hour gains are implied only if actual hours fell as scheduled, which was not measured. Sickness absence and resignations fell substantially, though without a control group or season-matched baseline these changes cannot be attributed to the schedule alone. The results are encouraging for office and knowledge work and more equivocal elsewhere.

The recommendations to add a comparison group, collect actual hours, use objective output measures, and run longer follow-up are the right ones. They should be presented as conditions for the paper's claims, not as refinements for future work.

I can draft a revised Summary, Discussion, and Conclusion along these lines, or a short referee report.
